intro:
Deli phone orders can pile up fast, especially during lunch. An AI phone host can answer the phone, take the order, and send it straight to the kitchen screen while your counter team keeps serving in person.

For delis and sandwich shops, that means fewer missed pickup calls, fewer repeat questions, and less time spent shouting over the slicer. ROAL is built for that kind of rush, and it works from your live menu, hours, and store info.

sections.h2: What kinds of deli phone orders can an AI host take?
sections.body:
A deli phone host works best when the order is simple but still has plenty of detail: bread choice, size, cheese, toppings, dressing, hot or cold, and special notes. It can take pickup and delivery orders from the restaurant’s live menu, then confirm the full order back before sending it to the kitchen screen.

For a sandwich shop, that matters because most calls are not complicated, but they still take time. A caller might say: "Turkey on rye, toasted, no tomato, add pickles, and make it a combo." The host can capture that, ask for the name and phone number, and quote a ready time.

A practical deli checklist for the phone:
- Sandwich size or roll choice
- Protein, cheese, and toppings
- Toasted or not toasted
- Hot or cold
- Pickup or delivery
- Caller name and phone number
- Any special notes

ROAL also avoids offering items marked sold out, so the phone host is working from what you can actually make. That helps keep the call accurate when the lunch rush is moving and the line is already long.

sections.body:

sections.h2: What should the phone say when a deli customer calls?
sections.body:
The best phone script is short and clear. Deli callers usually want speed, not a long greeting. The host should answer, take the order, and move on without making the caller repeat basic details.

A good opening line sounds like this: "Thanks for calling Main Street Deli. Would you like pickup or delivery?" From there, the host can ask for the sandwich, size, bread, toppings, and name.

Here is a simple flow you can use:
- Greet the caller and identify the shop.
- Ask pickup or delivery.
- Take the item, size, modifiers, and notes.
- Collect name and phone number.
- Quote a ready time.
- Confirm the full order back.

ROAL can also speak the caller’s language, which helps when your neighborhood has regulars who prefer something other than English. And if the caller asks for catering, has an allergy-sensitive question, wants a manager, or complains about an order, the host hands it to staff with a summary. That keeps the staff in control when the call gets complicated.

sections.h2: How much does phone answering cost compared with other options?
sections.body:
For deli owners, the cost question is often the biggest one. Third-party delivery apps commonly charge restaurants roughly 15-30% commission per order. Human answering services usually bill per minute or per call. Many AI phone answering products charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often around $79 to $599, whether or not orders come in.

ROAL uses a different model: $0.90 per completed phone order, meaning a confirmed order whose ticket reached the kitchen screen. There is no monthly fee, setup fee, per-minute fee, or contract. Calls, questions, and test calls are unlimited and free, and billing is monthly.

sections.h2: How do I forward my deli’s existing phone number?
sections.body:
You do not have to give up your current number. Once you claim the host, ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and you forward your restaurant’s existing number to it. You can forward all calls, or only when busy or unanswered, and you can turn forwarding off any time.

The exact steps depend on your carrier or phone system. On many landlines and some carriers, dialing *72 then the forwarding number forwards all calls, and *73 turns it off. On GSM mobile carriers like AT&T and T-Mobile, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off; **61*number# forwards unanswered calls and **67*number# forwards busy calls. Verizon Wireless uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually set forwarding in the web portal.

Always confirm the code with your carrier and test it with a call. A quick shop checklist:
- Call your own number from a cell phone.
- Confirm the host answers.
- Place a test order.
- Check that the ticket appears on the kitchen screen.
- Turn forwarding off and back on once so staff knows how it works.

If you want carrier-specific reminders, [Call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes) is a useful reference.

sections.h2: What does the kitchen and owner dashboard look like after calls come in?
sections.body:
The point of the dashboard is to keep the phone work organized, not buried. ROAL gives you live kitchen tickets with statuses like new, preparing, and ready. It also keeps call history with transcripts and recordings, plus a menu editor, hours, FAQs, upsell suggestions, and multi-location menus.

That matters for delis because lunch orders often need quick review. Maybe a caller asked for extra meat, a different bread, or a side that was easy to miss while the counter was busy. The transcript lets you check what was said, and the kitchen ticket keeps the order readable.

Use this simple end-of-shift review:
- Check new tickets and move them as you prep.
- Listen to any confusing calls.
- Fix menu wording if people keep asking the same thing.
- Add an FAQ for common questions like parking or hours.
- Mark sold-out items so the host stops offering them.

The owner can also answer questions the host could not answer once, and the host knows it from then on. That saves time on repeat calls. For owners comparing options, [AI phone host vs hiring phone staff](/compare/hiring-phone-staff) and [AI phone host vs answering service](/compare/answering-service) are good next reads.

sections.h2: What should a deli owner watch out for before going live?
sections.body:
A phone host can help a lot, but it is still important to set clear rules. ROAL does not take card numbers over the phone, so payment happens at pickup or however your restaurant already takes it. It also routes allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, catering requests, and manager requests to staff with a summary.

Before you go live, make sure these items are ready:
- Your menu is current.
- Sold-out items are marked sold out.
- Hours and address are correct.
- The phone host name and voice fit your shop.
- Staff know where the tickets show up.
- Someone on the team knows how to answer forwarded calls if needed.

For a deli, the small details matter. If you sell breakfast sandwiches until 11, make sure that is in the menu or hours. If you close early on Sunday, say so clearly. If parking is behind the building, add it. The better your public info is, the better the phone host will sound.

If you want to try it with your own menu, [build a free test host from your website](/try). ROAL is pre-launch, so the honest way to judge it is by testing it with your own calls, your own menu, and your own team.
